title: The Visual Guide to Incorporating AI into Today's Classrooms
author: Nick Potkalitsky
summary: Potkalitsky argues that charts, maps and diagrams are useful thinking tools for the AI-and-education moment, and he walks through four visual models for an AI-responsive writing curriculum. They are Amanda Bickerstaff's yes, yes-but and no decision tree for students, Jessica Parker's spiraling coil built around negotiating meaning, his own parallel circuit separating traditional writing skills from new AI competencies for middle and high school, and a double-loop learning cycle from engineering research. He frames the differences as complementary rather than competing. The piece is partly a personal prelude on cartography, and the models are mostly drawn from others, but the through-line is a practical case for giving teachers and students shared maps for when and how to use generative AI in writing.
points: Visual models act as cognitive maps for teachers and students and, used comparatively, help build an AI-responsive writing curriculum.
Bickerstaff's decision tree gives immediate guidance on when students should use AI, use it with caution, or avoid it.
Parker's concept of meaning negotiation reframes AI-assisted writing as a collaborative process in which the student stays the final authority.
Potkalitsky's parallel circuit keeps foundational writing skills distinct from new AI competencies such as prompting, AI search and ethics, for middle and high school settings.
The double-loop model shows the current AI curriculum conversation draws on design and learning scholarship that predates large language models.
quotes: As my prelude suggests, these charts play important functions beyond gathering together talking points, organizing concepts, or mapping out possible workflows. When employed in a comparative and collaborative manner, these tools acquire an agent-like role, assisting in the development of the AI-responsive writing curriculum that both we and our students seek

This diagram serves as a cognitive map for both teachers and students, guiding their engagement with AI. The degree to which students embrace and apply this framework will be indicative of the effectiveness of AI literacy and AI-responsive writing curricula.

Fundamentally, I’d argue that all AI-assisted writing can be viewed as a negotiation of meaning. This negotiation, somewhat ironically, occurs with tools that, currently, do not fully grasp meaning in the human sense.
The real challenge remains how to teach students to effectively negotiate meaning with AI. Here, Parker’s model emerges as a promising start, particularly apt for college-level students and higher.

On the left side of my model, I outline the traditional skills of a conventional writing curriculum, which form the bedrock for students to effectively engage with AI, a process that, in turn, further enhances these foundational skills. On the right side, I detail the new competencies necessary for optimizing large language models. These include basic AI literacy, prompt engineering, AI search techniques, conversational skills with AI, and understanding AI ethics.

At its core, this model illustrates the merging of knowledge-driven and information-driven processes within the act of writing. It underscores that writing decisions often run on parallel and sometimes conflicting paths, and resolving these often necessitates referring to a higher level of purpose, criteria, or objective to produce a satisfactory outcome.

Rather than perceiving these visions as conflicting, I encourage my readers to embrace the splendid diversity they represent. This multifaceted endeavor requires collective effort to craft effective, engaging, and ethical solutions for our students.
